explanation: Idògbé brought the unusual arrest upon himself. The passage clearly states that his sitting outside in dirty work clothes beyond the boundary (dotí kojá ààlà) was the direct cause of the police sweeping him up along with the thieves operating in the next neighborhood. Jókòótadé was merely the cousin sent to buy akara, and Jéjéniwà was Idògbé's uncle, neither involved in the arrest. Mèmúnà is simply identified as Idògbé's mother with no role in the incident.

Elégiri in this passage refers to thieves (olè). The context shows the police arrested Idògbé together with the elégiri who were operating (sosé) in the neighboring area, meaning these were criminals or robbers. Olópàá means police, who did the arresting rather than being arrested. Mékániki (mechanic) is Idògbé's own profession, and alákàrà sells akara — neither fits the criminal context described.

Alágemo (the chameleon) is the correct answer because the passage uses the chameleon as a metaphor for the suffering woman, describing how she used to carry loads like the chameleon (rù hangogo bí alágęemọ) during her period of barrenness. The passage describes all those painful behaviors — rubbing osun on walls, chasing children, fake crying — as characteristics of her barren period. Adáhunse and Aàfáà are the diviners/herbalists she consulted, not the barren person herself.

Igbà òdá refers to a period of sickness (àisàn). The proverb at the opening — one day's rain overcoming drought — sets the tone of suffering giving way to relief, and the passage describes how the woman moved from illness and misery (likened to an olókůnrùn, a sick person) to joy. While àirómobí (childlessness) is central to her story, the word òdá specifically points to the broader suffering/illness state, not barrenness alone. Aijeun and àisanra describe hunger and thinness, which are symptoms rather than the primary reference.

Adáhunse is who they sought help from. The passage explicitly states the woman was going about consulting ààfáà and adáhunse (à ń ya ojúlé ààfáà àti adáhunse kiri) during her period of barrenness and suffering. Adáhunse is a Yoruba traditional healer or diviner. Ajéwole is the husband who eventually forgot her suffering, olókůnrùn means a sick person used as a simile, and alágemo (chameleon) is also used as a comparison — neither was consulted.

The sweetness after bitterness was recovery from illness (bibó nínú àisàn). In the context of this passage, ewúro (bitterness) refers to the entire ordeal of suffering — sickness, barrenness, and misery — and the adùn (sweetness) is deliverance from that suffering state. While having children (rírí omo bí) is part of the story, the specific expression adùn tí ó gbèyin ewúro points to emerging from the illness and hardship described throughout the passage. Breaking a fast and having peace are unrelated to the central theme.

Aàfin oba ilú mi (The palace of my town's king) suits a descriptive essay (asàpèjúwe) because it invites the writer to paint a vivid picture of a physical place — its appearance, surroundings, and features. Owó kò níran (Money has no relatives) is argumentative or expository, requiring the writer to debate or explain a viewpoint. İmótótó (Cleanliness) is typically an expository topic. Ayeye ojó ibí mi tí ó kojá (My past birthday) leans narrative rather than purely descriptive.

İkíni ibèrè (opening greeting/salutation) is the third step in an informal Yoruba letter. The standard structure begins with the writer's address, then the date, and third comes the salutation/greeting before the body of the letter. Adírési àkọlétà (address of the letter) is first, and Akolé létà (title/heading) and Orúko akolétà (writer's name) come at other positions — not third. Getting this order right is essential for scoring full marks in letter writing.

Ékó ilé (home education or home training) is a title for a descriptive essay (asàpèjúwe) because it requires the writer to describe what home upbringing looks like, the environment, methods, and experiences involved. Aşàríyànriyàn is argumentative/debate, requiring taking a position. Asotàn is narrative/story form, and ajemó-işipayá is an expository or revealing essay — none match a topic that calls for describing the nature and setting of home education.

Onílétà (letter essay/epistolary form) is the essay type where two people speak in turns (síşè-n-tèlé), because a letter exchange involves one person writing and the other replying, alternating back and forth. Aşàríyànjiyàn is a debate which could involve two people but follows a formal argument structure, not alternating correspondence. Onísorògbèsi involves discussion/dialogue, but the specific sísè-n-tèlé pattern of taking turns most precisely describes letter writing. Ajemó-isípayá is an expository/revelatory essay with no inherent two-person structure.

Ìpín sílébù means dividing a word into syllables. In Yoruba, the nasal consonant 'n' can stand alone as its own syllable (syllabic nasal), so it must be separated when dividing words. Option C (pe-n ke-le-mee-si) correctly isolates 'n' as a standalone syllable and groups 'mee' as one unit reflecting its vowel length. Options A and B wrongly attach 'n' to adjacent syllables rather than treating it as an independent unit, which breaks the syllabic nasal rule.

Kónsónánti àfàfàséfètèpè describes a consonant produced with friction at the glottal or back-throat area of the mouth. The sound [h] is produced entirely at the glottis with air friction and no involvement of lips or teeth, fitting this classification precisely. [b] is a bilabial plosive produced by closing both lips, [f] is a labiodental fricative involving the upper teeth and lower lip, and [w] is a labiovelar approximant — all of these involve the front of the mouth. Only [h] matches the specific articulation described by àfàfàséfètèpè.

Àrànmó wáyé refers to words formed purely from within the Yoruba language using internal word-building processes, without borrowing from any outside language. Etilé is built entirely from native Yoruba elements meaning 'inside the house,' making it a product of internal word formation. İjúùbà is a greeting form, Awítúnwí involves a different derivational process, and Omoota is a compound noun — none of these specifically demonstrate àrànmó wáyé the way Etilé does. Etilé is the best example of a word that originated and was shaped entirely within the Yoruba linguistic system.

Isàmúlò àfòmó concerns how pronouns function and are embedded in Yoruba word structure and usage. Woléwolé illustrates àfòmó usage because a pronoun is incorporated into its formation, showing how pronouns interact with verbs and nouns in Yoruba grammatical construction. Omooba (prince), Aròko (essay/letter), and Aráalé (household member) are noun compounds that do not demonstrate pronoun usage in their formation or function. Woléwolé is therefore the option that most directly illustrates the application of àfòmó as taught in Yoruba grammar.

Oro àyálò afetiyá refers to a word borrowed into Yoruba from a foreign language outside the African linguistic family. Pétérù is the Yoruba phonological adaptation of the Latin/Greek name Petrus (Peter), and it represents a clear case of a foreign name borrowed and shaped to fit Yoruba sound patterns. While Esítéri (Esther) and Bíbéli or Báíbù (Bible) are also borrowed words, Pétérù most specifically exemplifies the àyálò afetiyá borrowing pattern being tested. The way the word is phonologically restructured to fit Yoruba syllable rules confirms it as the target example.

In the sentence 'Wón tan iná sinú ilé, ó mó roro,' the word 'roro' names the resulting condition — brightness or clarity — after the fire was lit, functioning as a noun. As oro-orúko (noun), it serves as the complement of the verb 'mó,' naming the state that came to be. Oro-işe (verb) is wrong because 'roro' here performs no action. Oro-àpónlé (adjective) does not apply because 'roro' is not modifying any noun; it stands independently as the named quality that resulted from the action.

In 'Adé àti Öjó lo wa isu lóko,' the word 'àti' links two noun subjects together. In the Yoruba grammar framework used in this curriculum, 'àti' is classified as orò-àpónlé because it functions as a joining or connecting particle between sentence elements. While oro-àsopò (conjunction) may seem appropriate, the specific Yoruba grammatical category being applied here places 'àti' under orò-àpónlé. Oro-işe and oro-àpėjúwe are clearly wrong because 'àti' is neither a verb nor an adverb in any usage.

In 'E rò wá ro ire o,' the verb 'rò' is used in a command that causes the listeners to perform a mental action, which classifies it as aşòkùnfà — a verb type that induces or causes an action to happen in another person. The imperative 'E rò' (all of you think/ponder) shows the speaker compelling others to act, which is the defining feature of aşòkùnfà. Elélà refers to a transitive verb, alápèpadà covers reversive action, and asòlůwàdàbo describes reflexive verbs — none capture the causative role 'rò' plays in this sentence.

In 'Bí mo bá lówó màá kólé,' the sentence splits into a subordinate conditional clause and a main clause. The olórí awé-gbólóhùn (main clause) must be able to stand alone and carry independent meaning — 'mo kólé' (I build a house) fulfils this because it contains both subject and predicate and expresses a complete thought. 'Bí mo bá lówó' is the dependent conditional clause meaning 'if I have money' and cannot stand alone. Option D 'màá kólé' is only the verb phrase without a stated subject, so it is incomplete as a full clause on its own.

The English phrase 'It is a sensitive issue' means it is a matter requiring careful attention and awareness from those handling it. Option D, 'Ó jé orò tó gba akíyèsí,' translates as 'It is a matter that deserves notice and careful attention,' which is the most accurate Yoruba equivalent. Option C, 'Ó jé oro elegé,' means 'It is a delicate matter,' which emphasises fragility rather than the need for thoughtful attention. Option B, 'Ó jé orò tó gba èrò,' means only 'It requires thought,' which is narrower than what 'sensitive' conveys in this context.

Àpètúnpě refers to word derivation through compounding — joining two or more base words to form a new one. 'Omokùnrin' is formed by combining 'omo' (child) and 'okùnrin' (male), making it a classic example of àpètúnpě. 'Atije' is a simple derivative meaning food consumed before a meal, while 'Ösoosè' means weekly and 'Åsejù' means excess — none of these involve compounding two full root words the way 'Omokùnrin' does.

'Ejan bákàn' is a Yoruba proverb (owe) that uses figurative meaning to convey a deeper truth about sudden or unexpected situations. Owe (proverbs) are short, wise sayings drawn from everyday experience, and this expression fits that category perfectly. It is not àdàpè (nickname), åkànlò-èdè (figure of speech), or ègó (riddle) because those have distinct structural and functional differences from the compressed wisdom form of owe.

Option C, 'İşoro wà nínú àwùjo,' most accurately translates 'This is a societal problem' — it conveys that a problem exists within society without distorting the meaning. Option A uses 'isòro' (with a different tonal mark) and drops the locative sense. Option B adds 'ai èyí' which is grammatically awkward and changes the sentence structure. Option D reverses the subject-predicate order in a way that alters emphasis, saying 'society has a problem' rather than placing the problem centrally.

Option C, 'Mamá mi rántí opolopò itàn àtijó,' correctly translates 'My mother recalled many old stories' because 'rántí' means to remember or recall, which matches the English verb exactly. Option A uses 'ronú sí' which means to think about or reflect, not to recall. Option B is grammatically incomplete and garbled. Option D uses 'so' meaning to say or tell, which changes the action from recalling to narrating.

In Yoruba oral tradition, 'ofo' are incantatory words or verbal charms meant to invoke protective or spiritual power. 'E kú iwájú o' in a literary-ritual context functions as an ofo — spoken to empower or protect someone moving forward into danger or the unknown, not merely as casual greeting. 'Ikíni' is everyday greeting, 'iwúre' is blessing or prayer, and 'oriki' is praise poetry — none carry the incantatory power structure that classifies this expression as ofo.

'Ibi tía ní kí gbégbé ó má gbé é ibè níí gbé' is an ofo (incantation) because it invokes a reversal of fate using ritual speech — directing misfortune away from the speaker by naming and redirecting it. The sentence structure, with its imperative spiritual force, marks it as ofo rather than common proverb or insult. 'Èebú' is an insult or curse spoken in anger, 'aló' is a folktale, and while ofo and èebú may overlap, ofo here is the precise term for this type of protective verbal charm.

In the story 'Ijàpà Tirókò Oko Yánnibo,' it was Okété (the giant pouched rat) who first ate pounded yam (iyán) with Ijàpà (the tortoise). This early alliance between Okété and Ijàpà drives part of the plot's social and moral dynamics. Oyà, Etu (antelope), and Igbíne are other characters in the story but were not the first to share the meal with Ijàpà as narrated in that episode.

In the story involving Ijàpà and Oro-Irókò, Ijàpà asked Oro-Irókò to beat him with a club (kùmò) — a trickster's request designed to achieve a hidden goal through apparent self-harm. This reflects Ijàpà's characteristic cunning; he uses an unusual request to manipulate the situation to his advantage. The other options — killing Oyà, sending Etu, or performing a different act — do not match what Ijàpà strategically requested from Oro-Irókò in this tale.

In the story 'Adígbónránkú, Ekùn, Ajá àti Jàpà,' it was Adígbónránkú that Ijàpà visited first at the blacksmith's forge (àgbède). The sequence of visits is a key narrative detail in this tale, and Adígbónránkú comes first in the order of encounters. Ekùn (leopard) and Ajá (dog) are also characters in the story, while Yánníbo is a place name — none of them are the first character Ijàpà encounters at the forge.

In W. Abímbólá's 'Àwon Ojú Odù Mérèerindínkógún,' it is Ifá — the oracle and embodiment of divine wisdom — who went to war at tentèsín. This reflects Ifá's role not just as a passive divination force but as an active spiritual agent in Yoruba cosmology. Awo (the diviner) serves Ifá but does not replace him in this narrative role; Oyèwón and Aparún are other figures in the poems but are not identified as the one who went to this particular war.

In Odu Obara Meji, the awo (diviners) instructed Bara to dwell on Oko alerò odun, which means the farm that provides seasonal shelter and abundance. This location symbolizes provision, security, and renewal for Bara throughout the year. Oko aláwo refers to the diviner's own farm, while Eyin odi means behind a wall, and Odo ebora is the river of spirits — none of these match the specific instruction given in the text. The awo's advice to settle on Oko alerò odun carries spiritual and practical significance for Bara's wellbeing.

The expression Omọ àwúşè, ará ilágbède identifies someone from the Olofà lineage, as the text uses ancestral markers tied to that specific clan. In Eégún Aláré, Ògúnníran uses such praise identifications to establish where characters come from socially and geographically. Arèsà, Onikòyí, and Orímóògùnjé are other distinct groups or characters in the play whose identities do not match this particular description. Understanding these clan markers helps readers track character relationships and conflicts in the drama.

In Eégún Aláré, Jeládé competed directly against Dúdúyemí, and this rivalry forms one of the central dramatic tensions in the play. Ògúnníran presents this contest to highlight themes of talent, identity, and social competition among the characters. Dásofúnjó, Ojékúnlé, and Orimóògùnjé are other characters with their own roles in the plot but were not Jeládé's opponent in this specific contest. Recognising which characters are in direct conflict with each other is key to understanding the structure of the play.

Jè-Lárinnàká is another name for Dúdúyemí in the play Eégún Aláré, showing how Ògúnníran uses dual naming to give characters deeper identity and praise-name significance. This technique is common in Yoruba literary tradition where a character may be called by a personal name and also by a descriptive or lineage-based name. Ojékúnlé, Dáşofúnjó, and Orimóògùnjé are separate characters in the drama with their own identities and should not be confused with Jè-Lárinnàká. Students must pay attention to how these names are used interchangeably in the text.

Ögúngbèmí laughed with such deep emotion that tears ran from his eyes specifically upon seeing his child, showing the overwhelming joy of reunion between parent and child in the story Ojú Rí. This scene demonstrates the power of parental love as a theme in the text. His head turning and feeling generally happy are too vague and do not match the specific trigger described by Òní. Receiving money would suggest a materialistic motive, which contradicts the emotional context of the scene.

In the prose narrative Ojú Rí, the text specifically states that Iná-ń-ió built his house in the Oko-Oba area of Lagos. This detail about setting helps ground the story in a recognisable Lagos geography and gives context to the characters' social circumstances. Agége, Abúlé-Egbá, and Isolo are all real Lagos neighbourhoods but are not the location mentioned in this part of the story. Students must read carefully to distinguish between real places mentioned as background and the specific location relevant to each character.

Ogúngbèmí and Ogúnlabí are specifically named in Ojú Rí as the two who carried out fraudulent activities together in Lagos. This partnership in jibiti (fraud/deception) is central to understanding Ogúngbèmí's moral downfall in the narrative. Ogún-Åjobo, Kàbírů, and Délé are other characters in the story but the text does not link them to Ogúnlabí in this particular crime. Identifying who partners with whom in dishonest acts helps students trace the consequences that follow in the plot.

In the poem Wón ń wò yín, the èèwò (taboo) committed by the father was prostrating (dòbálè) before his own child, which violates the fundamental Yoruba social order where parents hold authority and children owe them deep respect. This inversion of roles is treated as a serious abomination in Yoruba cultural values. Beating a child, cutting a child, or drinking to excess are not what the poem identifies as the taboo action. Adébòwálé uses this image to show how the natural order of family and society can be dangerously disrupted.

The central lesson of the poem Bíntín Layé is that we should wayé máyà oot níwonba, meaning we should live life with moderation, caution, and contentment rather than excess or recklessness. Adébòwálé warns that a life lived without restraint leads to regret and destruction. Simply enjoying oneself or avoiding hardship does not capture the poem's full message about disciplined and measured living. Doing one's little bit (se iwonba ti wa) is closer but still misses the specific call to live cautiously and moderately in all things.

In the poem title Wón ń wò yín, the subject wón refers to edun, the colobus monkey, which is the central figure being used to observe and reflect on human behaviour. Adébòwálé employs the monkey as a literary device to comment on society from an external vantage point. Omo (child), esin (horse), and òbí (kola nut) each carry their own symbolic weight in Yoruba literature but are not what wón refers to in this particular poem. Recognising this animal reference is essential to interpreting the poem's meaning and tone correctly.

Oláwùmí called Mojèrè 'omo ijoba' because Mojèrè was suspected of acting as a government informant or spy within the community in the play Ìyàwó Alárédè. This accusation reflected distrust of Mojèrè's loyalty to the people around her. Dàpò, Fúnmi, and Oládélé were all characters in the play but none of them received this specific label from Oláwùmí. To answer this correctly, you must follow character relationships and dialogue closely in the text.

Màmá Ségun traveled to Ôsogbo to attend the wedding of her husband's friend (oré oko rè), not her own relative or child. The options àbúrò rè (her younger sibling) and àbúrò oko rè (her husband's younger sibling) both describe family members, not friends. Omo rè (her child) is also wrong because no such event involving her child is described. The play makes clear the social connection is through her husband, not blood relation.

Mojèrè's true and original love interest in the play was Atéré, and the plot builds tension around this emotional attachment. Adéyemo, Oládélé, and Oláwùmí were all characters she interacted with, but none held her deepest romantic feelings. Understanding who Mojèrè truly loved is central to grasping the conflict in the story. Confusing Oládélé or Oláwùmí with Atéré would come from not reading the play carefully enough.

Onígbàjámo is the craftsman in Yoruba tradition who specifically makes the hoe (okó) and related farm implements. Alágbèdé is a general blacksmith who works with metal but is not the specialist associated with making hoes. Aláró is a cloth-dyer whose work has nothing to do with farming tools, and Olóólà is a barber and circumciser. Knowing the distinct roles of traditional Yoruba craftsmen is key to answering this question.

Bojúbojú, the Yoruba version of hide and seek, is a moonlight game (eré òṣupá) because children traditionally played it outdoors at night when moonlight provided enough visibility. Ayò is a strategy board game played with seeds during the day, not a moonlight activity. Òkòtó means snail and is not a game at all. Àrín refers to a different kind of activity unrelated to moonlight play.

Yétúndé means 'mother has returned,' directly expressing the Yoruba belief in reincarnation (isèyinwáyé), where a deceased ancestor is believed to have returned in a newborn child. Names like Adébóyè ('the crown brings honor') and Àtàndá reflect royalty and circumstance but carry no reincarnation meaning. Tààbì is also unrelated to the concept of returning from death. Whenever you see a name meaning someone 'has returned,' it points to isèyinwáyé.

Ìwòfà is the specific Yoruba term for a person who pawns themselves (singbà) as labor to repay a debt, working for the creditor until the debt is cleared. Erú means slave, which is a permanent condition with no agreement for release, making it different from ìwòfà. Onígbòwó is the creditor or moneylender — the opposite role in the transaction. Alárinnà means a traveler and has no connection to debt or pledging oneself.

In ancient Yoruba culture, male children were given their names on the ninth day (ọjọ kesàn-án) after birth, which was the customary time set aside for naming boys. Female children were named on the seventh day, which is why keje (seventh) is wrong — it applies to girls, not boys. Karùn-ún (fifth) and kęjo (eighth) were not traditional naming days in Yoruba custom. Remembering the difference: seven for girls, nine for boys.

Ààlè is a recognized method of self-help and protection in Yoruba tradition, used to guard one's property or interests through cultural and spiritual boundary-marking. Àáró is communal farm labor where neighbors help each other on the farm, which is a different type of cooperative activity. Işíde and işipà describe other ceremonial or labor contexts that do not fit the specific category of ìran-ara-eni-lówó being tested here. Understanding the distinctions between these Yoruba social practices is essential.

In Yoruba custom, sending a broom (òòyà) to a friend was a cultural way of signaling that you wished to visit or see that person, serving as a friendly message of invitation. It was not a way of ending a friendship — that would require a different symbolic act or direct statement. Wanting to marry someone or pointing out their mistake would be communicated very differently in Yoruba tradition. The broom here carries a warm, social meaning, not a hostile or romantic one.

Yéwándé is the youngest because the passage explicitly names her 'làbikéyin won lénjélénje,' which means the very last-born of all the children. Kládé is identified as firstborn (làkóbí), Ådůké as second (làtèlé), and Kólájo as third (omo keta). Since birth order is stated for each child, Yéwándé is definitively the youngest. Kóládé being oldest rules out option A, while B and C are middle children.

The passage directly states 'Mésidisi ni ó máa ń gbé lo síbi isé,' meaning Awódélé habitually uses his Mercedes to go to work. The Jeep is reserved only for special or important journeys, not daily commuting. Pijó and Tòyótà are mentioned as part of his fleet but are never linked to his work trips. The Yoruba word 'máa ń gbé lo' shows a regular habit, confirming Mercedes is his work vehicle.

The passage states Awódélé has been in his prosperity for 'odún méwàá gbáko,' meaning a full ten years, making kéwàá the correct answer. Things began going well for him three years after his father's death, and he has now sustained that wealth for ten years. Options kétàlá (13), keje (7), and keta (3) do not correspond to the ten-year duration the passage emphasises as the measure of his current successful period.

The best title is 'Edá kò láròpin' (Human potential has no limit) because the whole passage shows Awódélé rising from the son of a beggar to a wealthy man with six cars, accomplished children, and community respect. This central message of limitless human progress cannot be captured by the narrow titles about his cars or his children alone. 'Ikú alágbe' completely misrepresents the story since no death occurs and the theme is success, not loss.

The root cause of Àlàó's near-death was his reckless, immoral lifestyle — the passage says he wore immorality like clothing ('gbé iwà isekúse wò bí èwù') and was nearly driven to living like a madman on the streets. This path of reckless living led directly to his crisis. Taking poison (option A) was the method of the attempt, not the cause. Options B and D describe his father's efforts and a medical test, which are surrounding events, not the cause.

The phrase 'Gbogbo rè se wékú bí idodo èfon' compares Awódélé's household to soldiers in uniform — perfectly level and matched — so 'wékú' means dógba (equal or matched). The simile 'bí idodo èfon' (like a soldier's uniform) reinforces the idea of uniformity and equality. Options jora (resemble), dára (good/fine), and yanjú (excel/succeed) each miss this specific meaning of being evenly matched or equal in all respects.

Àkàndé spoke the proverb 'orí òkéré koko láwo, báa wí fómo eni a gbo' as a lament over his son Àlàó's disobedience, because every effort he made to raise Àlàó properly had ended in failure. The proverb means that a child who is warned should listen, implying Àlàó refused to heed good guidance. Options B, C, and D describe how the mother spoiled him, the poison he took, and his medical test — these are consequences and events, not the specific trigger that caused the father to utter the proverb.

The passage says Iyápé had been indulging Àlàó 'nítorí pé ó jé ògúnná kan soso ti ó ní,' meaning because Àlàó was the only child she had. Therefore 'ògúnná kan soso' (only child) refers to Àlàó himself, not his mother. Iyápé is the mother who possesses the only child; she is not described as someone's only child in the passage. Alákátá is not a person's name but a word describing a wayward, irresponsible way of life.

An essay titled 'Igi òpe' (The Palm Tree) is expository writing (ajemó-isípayá) because its purpose is to reveal and explain the tree's characteristics, parts, and uses to inform the reader. Aşàpèjůwe (descriptive) focuses mainly on painting a sensory picture of appearance rather than explaining information. Aşàríyànjiyàn (argumentative) takes a position and debates it, while oníròyìn (narrative) tells a story — neither matches an informational essay about a plant.

The consequence of Àlàó's reckless and immoral lifestyle was contracting an incurable, shameful disease (O kó àrùn-kògbóògùn) — the medical examination (ayèwò) revealed a condition so disgraceful that he chose to attempt suicide rather than live with the shame. Option A (living as a madman) was a near-consequence the passage describes him almost reaching, not the final outcome. Option B (speaking a proverb) was his father's action, and option D (being from Okè-Egan) was already stated at the beginning of the passage as an existing fact.

The passage is a news story (aroko oniroyin) about Alao who became depressed and swallowed poison, landing in hospital. 'Ojo kan ti aye su mi' meaning 'A day life frustrated me' best captures the emotional core of this specific event and suits a news headline. 'Aye odi-oni' is too vague and general to serve as a focused news title. 'Epo isebe' has nothing whatsoever to do with the content of the passage. A good news headline must reflect the central incident being reported.

In Yoruba phonology, front vowels (faweli iwaju) are produced with the tongue positioned toward the front of the mouth. [e] qualifies as a front vowel because air flows through the front part of the oral cavity during its production. Both [u] and [o] are back vowels, produced with the tongue drawn toward the back of the mouth. [a] is a central vowel, not front. Only [e] and [i] are classified as front vowels in Yoruba.

An informal letter (leta aigbagbefe) is distinguished from a formal letter by the fact that only the sender's address (adiresi agbaleta) appears at the top, not the recipient's address. Formal letters require both sender's address and the recipient's address (adiresi akoleta), but informal letters omit the recipient's address entirely. The greeting (ikini ibere) and the recipient's name (oruko akoleta) appear in both formal and informal letters, so they are not exclusive to informal letters. This makes adiresi agbaleta the only feature unique to the informal letter format.

The title 'Igba ojo dara ju igba erun lo' asserts that the rainy season is superior to the dry season, which is a debatable opinion rather than a statement of fact. This makes it an argumentative essay topic (asariyanjiya), because it presents a position that a writer must defend with evidence while acknowledging opposing views. A news essay (oniroyin) reports verified facts, not comparative opinions. A descriptive essay (asapejuwe) paints a picture without taking sides, and a narrative (ajemo-isipaya) tells a story rather than argues a point.

The consonant [gb] in Yoruba is produced by simultaneously closing both the lips (fete) and the back of the mouth at the soft palate (afafafase/velar position), making it a doubly articulated sound. This dual point of articulation classifies it as afafafasefetepe, meaning labial-velar. Afafaseepe would describe a sound made only at the velum, afejete-pe describes labiodental sounds like [f] or [v], and afajape refers to sounds made at the alveolar ridge like [d] or [n]. Because [gb] requires two simultaneous closures, option D is the only accurate classification.

The word 'ipeju-peju' can be divided into syllables as: i-pe-ju-pe-ju, which gives exactly five (marun-un) syllables. In Yoruba, each vowel sound typically forms its own syllable, making it easy to count by identifying each vowel unit. Options A (meta/three) and B (merin/four) undercount the syllables, while option D (mefa/six) overcounts. A careful syllable-by-syllable breakdown confirms five as the correct number.

When 'ku' and 'ale' combine to form 'kaale,' the vowel at the end of 'ku' is deleted during the joining process, which is the linguistic process called aanmeyin (elision). Aranmo afooro refers to adding a prefix to a word, which does not describe this process. Aranmo elebe refers to adding a suffix, which also does not apply here. Aanmeyin specifically names the dropping of a vowel at the boundary where two words meet, producing the shortened combined form 'kaale.'

Standard Yoruba words must carry tone marks that match recognized tone patterns for that word, and 'Agbon' with an acute accent on the first vowel A does not represent any valid Yoruba word. 'Agbon' without tone marking can represent coconut in certain contexts. 'Agbon' with a grave accent on the o (Agbon) is the correct Yoruba word for wasp. The acute tone on A in option C creates a tone pattern that does not exist for this word in the Yoruba lexicon, so it is not a proper Yoruba word.

Okuugbe (a Yoruba compound noun) is formed by directly joining two separate nouns together to create a new word with a unified meaning. Adding a middle affix (afooro), using repetition (apetunpe), or adding a prefix alone does not produce a compound noun in the same sense. The combination of two distinct nouns (kikan oro-oruko meji po) is what defines the okuugbe structure in Yoruba grammar. Options A, B, and C all describe modification of a single noun rather than the fusion of two.

In Yoruba, tone marks on identical-looking words distinguish completely different meanings. Ekun with a grave (low) tone on the u, written Ekun, refers to the leopard (eranko). Ekun with a high tone on both syllables means weeping, lamentation, or crying, not an animal. Options A, C, and D carry tone patterns that point to the word meaning tears or mourning. Only option B (Ekun with low tone on u) correctly identifies the wild animal known as the leopard.

In the sentence 'Adé lo sí oko,' the word 'sí' is an oro-atókùn, which is a particle or connecting word that shows direction or relationship between words. It does not describe anything (that would be oro-àpèjuwe), it is not a noun naming a person or thing (oro-orúko), and it is not a conjunction joining clauses (oro-àpónlé). Oro-atókùn words like 'sí,' 'ni,' and 'ti' connect parts of a sentence without carrying independent meaning on their own. Recognizing these small functional words is key to understanding Yoruba sentence structure.

The phrase 'ebà gbigbóná' is a noun phrase (àpólà orúko) because 'ebà' is a noun and 'gbigbóná' is an adjective modifying it, with the noun as the head word. A verb phrase (àpólà ise) would be headed by a verb showing action. An atókùn phrase would be led by a particle. Since the phrase names a thing (hot eba), it functions as a noun phrase and serves as the object in the full sentence.

In 'Bàbá Olú ti dé,' the word 'Olú' is an ajórúko, meaning it is a proper name used to identify a specific person. Ajórúko refers to personal names that distinguish one individual from another. It is not an asàpėjúwe, which would describe a quality, nor an asàfihàn, which points out or demonstrates a noun. Olú functions here to tell us exactly whose father arrived, making it clearly a proper noun.

The sentence 'Bọ́lá ra eja sè je' is an example of gbólóhùn olóro-ise, a verbal sentence, because the predicate is built around a series of verbs: ra (bought), sè (cooked), and je (ate). An alákànpò is a compound sentence joining two independent clauses, which is not the case here. An eléyo oro-ise contains a verbal subordinate clause, not the same as a string of serial verbs. The defining feature here is the chain of verbs all sharing one subject.

Option B, 'Bàbá mi kó lé márùn-ún,' is the correct direct translation because 'kó' is simple past tense meaning 'built,' and 'lé márùn-ún' means 'five houses.' Option C adds 'fé' which means 'wants to,' changing the meaning to a future intention. Option D uses 'ń gbiyànjú láti' meaning 'is trying to,' which is not what the English says. Option A uses an emphatic cleft construction that adds extra nuance not present in the original sentence.

A gbólóhùn àsodorúko (nominal clause) is a dependent clause that functions as a noun, often introduced by 'pé' in Yoruba. Option A contains 'pé Bùnmi ti dé,' which acts as the object of 'mò' (know), making the whole clause function like a noun phrase — that is a nominal clause. Option B contains a relative clause modifying a noun. Option C has an adverbial clause of time. Option D has a comparative clause introduced by 'bí,' not a nominal clause.

Option A, 'Ó lóra láti béèrè irànlówó,' best translates 'He was reluctant to ask for help' because 'lóra' directly means to be slow or reluctant, and 'irànlówó' means help or assistance. Option B uses 'àtiléyin' which means support rather than help, so it is slightly off. Options C and D use 'sòro fún un' meaning 'it was difficult for him,' which implies inability more than unwillingness, changing the nuance of the original sentence. Reluctance suggests an attitude, not a difficulty.

Option C, 'Orúko rere dára ju oro lọ,' correctly translates 'A good name is better than riches' because 'dára ju... lọ' is the Yoruba comparative structure meaning 'is better than,' and 'oro' means wealth or riches. Option A contains 'Onuko' which is not correct Yoruba for name. Option B says 'a good name is one's wealth,' which is a different idea entirely. Option D uses 'wùnmí' meaning 'I prefer' which is personal and subjective, not the same as 'is better than.'

The expression 'Mo wí wí wí, mo fo fo fo' is an example of àwitúnwí, which is deliberate repetition of words for emphasis or poetic effect. The words 'wí' and 'fo' are each repeated three times to intensify the action described. Iforodárà involves contrast or antithesis between two opposing ideas. Ifohunpèniyån likens a person's voice to something else. Àşorégèé is exaggeration or hyperbole, which is different from the structural repetition seen here.

Option B, 'Agbà tó jin sí kòtò, ojú re ló fó,' is not a proverb because it states a literal physical cause and effect — an elder who falls into a pit injures his eyes — rather than carrying a deeper moral or life lesson. A true owe (proverb) uses indirect, figurative language to teach a social truth. Options A, C, and D all carry symbolic meanings that apply broadly to human conduct and community values. The absence of metaphorical wisdom disqualifies option B from being a proverb.

In the story of Ijapa and the king's daughter, Kannakánná performed the task the king set better than all others and emerged the best, which is why option A is correct. The other animals like Ekùn (leopard), Asá (hawk), and Alákàn (crab) all attempted the task but could not match Kannakánná's performance. Ekùn was strong but that strength was not suited to the specific task. Understanding the plot of this text clearly shows Kannakánná as the outstanding performer.

The king made yam mound farming (kiko ebè işu) the condition for whoever wanted to marry his daughter, making option B correct. This farming task was used to test the strength and diligence of all the suitors. Option A about digging a good well, option C about climbing a tree, and option D about killing a leopard were not the tasks described in this story. The text specifically mentions agricultural labor as the king's requirement.

The phrase 'Okünrin kóróbótó bí oká' is an example of oriki because it uses a descriptive praise name that glorifies or characterizes a person, which is the hallmark of oriki in Yoruba oral literature. Aló refers to folktales or riddles, not praise poetry. Ofo refers to incantations used for specific purposes, while àwitúnwí refers to tongue twisters. Only oriki matches this style of attributing a striking characteristic to describe or honor someone.

In the odu Òtúúrúpòn Méji as presented by Abímbólá, it was Oyeepolu that the father abandoned carelessly (fi silè ní rèwerèwe), making option D correct. Teleni, Igbasoro, and Alapaandedę are other characters in the collection but they do not fit this specific role in that particular odu. The odu narrates how a father's negligence affected Oyeepolu. Reading the specific odu passage carefully reveals this detail.

The young man in the story told his family that he would become a hunter (ode), which is why option B is correct. He did not claim he would become a drummer (ìlù lílù), a singer (orin kíko), or a medicine man (oníṣègùn). His ambition was specifically hunting, which later connected him to his encounters with Ijapa in the story. This career choice drives the entire plot forward.

Òrúnmilà is referred to as the 'short man of Igeti hill' (okùnrin kúkúrú òkè Igeti) in Abímbólá's Awon Ojú Odù, making option C correct. Ogún is the deity of iron and war and is not associated with this description. Òòduà is the progenitor deity and Obàtálá is the deity of creation, neither of whom carries this specific epithet. Igeti is a place closely associated with Òrúnmilà in Ifá literary corpus.

In Eégún Aláré by Ögúnníran, it was Ológbojò who first wore or carried the masquerade costume (ru èkú eégun), making option C correct. Dúdúyemí, Láinnàká, and jelànàdé are all characters in the play but none of them performed this first act. The primacy of Ológbojò in this regard is a significant plot point that establishes the origin of the masquerade tradition in the drama. Students must follow the sequence of events in the play carefully.

The masquerade elders opposed Ojéládé's reintegration into normal society because he completely failed to show them respect or pay homage (kò júbà won rárá), making option D correct. Option A suggesting one of them wanted to take his wife, and option C suggesting he performed more powerful magic than them, are not the reason stated in the text. Showing respect to elders and authorities is a central theme in the play, and Ojéládé's failure to do this was the core offense. This conflict drives much of the drama's tension.

In the odu Ogúndá Méji, it was Aemole eekan who cast Ifa (difa) for Odyi òkòkó, making option D correct. Oge, Arugbo, and Ogun omo appear in other parts of Abímbólá's collection but are not the diviner in this specific odu. The identity of who performs Ifa divination in each odu is a key detail that students must memorize from the prescribed text. Careful reading of each odu's opening lines usually reveals who the diviner is.

Gbola refused to marry Titi because she was not enlightened or civilized (kò lajú), meaning she lacked exposure and modern awareness, which is why option D is correct. Option A saying she was disobedient, option B saying she was illiterate, and option C saying she was not beautiful do not match what the novel Olorunsogo presents as Gbola's reason. In the context of the novel, lajú relates to a person's level of exposure and sophistication. This detail reflects the tension between traditional upbringing and modern expectations in the story.

In Ögúnniran's play 'Eégún Alåré', Öjè Lárinnàká is established as the husband of İyádùn, making option B correct. Dáşofúnjó, Dúdúyemí, and Öjékúnlé are all characters in the play but none of them holds the role of İyádùn's husband. Students must pay close attention to character relationships when reading Yoruba dramatic texts for WAEC.

In Èsó-Olúborode's novel 'Olorunsogo', Fémi òòsàfúnminíyi is identified as Rónké's sweetheart during their secondary school days, making option C correct. Àbèfé Adéníyi, Àdisá Láyí, and Kúnlé Åmòsá are other male characters in the story but are not romantically linked to Rónké at school. Keeping track of romantic relationships between characters is important for WAEC Yoruba literature questions.

In Layiwola's poem 'Akòwé ko wúrà', the poet uses the image of 'Ode etilé' (a hunter who stays close to home, never venturing far) to compare the narrow-minded focus of the scholar who only values book knowledge. This metaphor criticizes someone who is educated but lacks broader wisdom and real-world experience. Ako irè, obe òsikí, and Eyin díndín are wrong because they do not capture the idea of limited scope or complacency that the poem criticizes.

In 'Olorunsogo', it was Ísúmáilà who beat Bídèmí so severely that she lost consciousness, making option A the correct answer. Oláníyi, Ésan, and Fémi are characters in the story but none of them is responsible for this violent act against Bídèmí. Remembering which character commits each action is essential for scoring in Yoruba literature comprehension.

In the poem 'Erò Lobèe Gbègiri', the poet states that whoever drinks garri (eba) before sleeping will dream of floating or swimming in a body of water — 'lálàá wakò ojú-omi' — because the starchy meal weighs heavily on the stomach and mind. Option A (yàgbé) and option C (lálàá wa kèké) do not match what the poem actually says about the dreamer's experience. This is a detail-focused question requiring close reading of the poem's imagery.

In Awé's play 'Ápótí Alákàrà', the sentence describes men chasing after Ańwòó the way a mother hen chases those who threaten her chicks, confirming option A is correct. The comparison 'àgbébò adię olómọ yoyo' (a protective mother hen) describes how desperately men pursue Ańwòó, highlighting her attractiveness. Abèó, Aàké, and Şèrí are other female characters in the play but this particular description belongs to Ańwòó.

In 'Ápótí Alákàrà', Öjògbede served as the chairman at Arówólò's graduation ceremony (ikékòó-gboyè), making option C correct. Kàrímù is a major character in the play but was not given this role, and Oyè is also present but does not chair the event. Students should note the social roles assigned to each character across the key scenes of the play.

In Layiwola's poem 'òle', the poet acknowledges that a lazy person does no work but possesses 'ariwo enu' — a loud, complaining mouth — as their most active tool, making option A correct. The poem uses irony to show that while the lazy person avoids labour, they are never silent in their excuses and noise. Ako ajá, ojú àánú, and oko lójúde are wrong because they do not match the specific attribute the poet assigns to the lazy character in this poem.

Among the options listed, only 'Ifaradà' (patience and endurance) qualifies as a good character trait (iwà rere), making option A correct. Ofófó means gossip, Olè means theft, and Imele refers to laziness or sluggishness — all of which are negative traits condemned in Yoruba cultural values. This question tests students' knowledge of Yoruba ethical concepts as taught in the ÀSA section of the curriculum.

In Awé's 'Ápótí Alákàrà', Àbèó is the wife of Kàrímù, the akara seller, making option D correct. Sèrí, Ańwòó, and Alàké are all female characters in the play but they do not share this marital relationship with Kàrímù. Knowing the family and household relationships between characters is a common area of examination in WAEC Yoruba drama questions.

Ilepa is a cultural practice done during Yoruba burial ceremonies (isinkú), where participants chase or pursue as part of the mourning and funeral rites. This practice is specifically tied to death and burial traditions in Yoruba culture, not to celebrations of new life or social gatherings. Igbéyàwó (marriage), isomolórúko (naming ceremony), and iranraenilówó (mutual financial assistance) are joyful occasions that do not involve ilepa.

Iserun refers to a household servant or helper who performs duties at the direction of a father or mother, so the person who serves you at the behest of your parents is your iserun. This word describes someone who works for you in a domestic or supportive capacity, fulfilling tasks your parents assign. Alábàárò is a companion or neighbor, olówó is a wealthy person or owner, and iwòfà is someone pawned as a pledge — none of these match the description of serving on behalf of parents.

In Yoruba tradition, sending osun (camwood paste) to someone is a culturally recognized way of announcing that a pregnant woman in the household has successfully given birth. Osun is associated with new life and is used in birth-related rituals, making option D the correct meaning. The message has nothing to do with an invitation to eat, the death of a friend, or the king summoning someone — those events use different cultural signals.

The taboo against a pregnant woman walking outdoors at midday (òsàn-án) is primarily a protective measure (aàbò) — Yoruba belief holds that evil spirits and dangerous forces are most active at noon and could harm the unborn child or the mother. The purpose of the restriction is safety and spiritual protection, not cleanliness (imótótó) or religious worship (èsin). Aàbò correctly captures the idea that the eewo exists to guard vulnerable persons from harm.

Erelú is a female title in Yoruba traditional governance, given to a titled woman of high standing in the community. Apènà is a male official in the Egungun masquerade society, Ajànà is a male title in the Ogboni/Osugbo institution, and Olúwo is the male head priest of the Ifá or related religious order. Only Erelú is feminine among the options.

The proverb 'Ìka tó bá sè loba ń gé' (the finger that misbehaves, the king cuts off) is directly about how offenders face punishment — it belongs to the tradition of arbitration, judgment, and the consequences of wrongdoing (òràn dídá àti ijiyà). It illustrates the authority of the king to punish crime, not anything related to greeting elders, communal labor, or sharing inheritance.

Odún Osun Osogbo is a traditional indigenous Yoruba festival celebrated in honor of the Osun deity, a river goddess, and has been practiced by the Yoruba long before contact with outside religions. Christmas (odún kérési) and Easter (odún àjíñde) are Christian celebrations brought by missionaries, while Eid (odún itúnu ààwè) is an Islamic observance — all three are foreign-origin festivals, not indigenous Yoruba ones.

The passage states clearly that Jenera Ayinlá was on a white horse and was singing for Egbé Idándè ('Orí esin funfun ni Jenera Ayinlá wà tó ń korin fún Egbé idándè'). Músílíù sang 'kísà' for a different group, and Idàgèrè sang 'sége' — neither of them performed for Egbé Idándè. Hárúnà Isòlá is mentioned only as Músílíù's father, not as a performer.

The passage describes Jenera Ayinlá as being on top of a white horse ('Orí esin funfun ni Jenera Ayinlá wà'), meaning he rode a horse (gun esin). He was singing for Egbé Idándè from atop the horse, but the question asks what he specifically did — riding the horse is what the text emphasizes about him. He did not personally go forward to greet the king (ki oba) nor is he described as dancing (jáde jó).

The word 'won' in the passage refers back to the various egbeegbé (groups/associations) that had come to dance before the king, such as Idándè, Omoladé, Ominira, and others. Throughout the passage, 'won' consistently refers to these associations and their members acting collectively. It does not point to the king (oba), an individual singer (akorin), or spectators (ònwòran), since the entire narrative describes the groups performing before the king.

Ìdàgèrè ni eléré ibílè nítorí àyokà náà sọ pé 'Eléré ibílè kan tí won ń pè ní İdàgèrè náà kọ sége lórin' — ọ̀rọ̀ tó fi hàn pé ó jẹ̀ aṣẹlú àṣà ìbílẹ̀. Músílíù jẹ́ akọrin tó kọ kísà, kò sí ìmọ̀ pé ó jẹ́ eléré ibílè. Hárúnà jẹ́ bàbá Músílíù nìkan. Àyinlá jẹ́ Jenera tó wà lórí ẹṣin funfun tó ń kọrin fún egbé kan.

Àkọlé 'Ayeye jó-kí-oba' bá àyokà yìí mu jù nítorí gbogbo ìtàn náà ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa àwọn egbé tó wá jó kí oba, àwọn akọrin tó tẹ̀lé wọn, àti bí ìgbádùn náà ṣe rí. 'Birà àwọn akorin' dín kù nítorí àyokà náà ò ṣàfihàn nìkan àwọn akọrin. 'Àwọn àlejò Kábíyèsí' kò tọ̀ nítorí àwọn egbé wọ̀nyí kì í ṣe àlejò òde òní.

Àròko ajem-işipayá nílò ojúiwoye ìfojúsùn àti ìrònú tó kọjá ohun tó wà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. 'Bí mo bá jẹ́ olórí orilè-edè yìí' jẹ́ ìfojúsùn àti ìyọjú-ara-ẹni sínú ipò tí kò sẹlẹ̀, èyí ní mímú àwọn ọmọ akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ lò ojú inú. Àwọn àkọlé bíi 'Ilé-ìtajà kan tí mo lọ' àti 'Ìrírí mi ní àdúgbò wa' jẹ́ ìtàn-ìrírí tó ti ṣẹlẹ̀. 'Bàbá wúlò ju ìyá lọ' jẹ́ àròko aláriyànjiyàn.

Àròko asàpèjúwe ń ṣapejuwe ènìyàn, ibi, tàbí nǹkan kan ní ọ̀nà àlàyé. 'Ilé àwọn Adémólá' jẹ́ apejuwe ibi kan pàtó, èyí ní bá ìdí àròko asàpèjúwe mu. 'Aşà ìbílẹ̀ dára ju àşà oyinbó lọ' jẹ́ àròko aláriyànjiyàn. 'Tí mo bá jẹ́ Ògá ilé-èkó' jẹ́ ajem-işipayá. 'Fáàrí àşejù' sọ̀rọ̀ nípa ìhùwàsí kan tí kì í ṣe apejuwe ibi tàbí nnkan kan pàtó.

Àsúnsí jẹ́ ohùn tí afẹ́fẹ́ ń jáde lọ nípasẹ̀ imú, ó sì ń ṣe àmúlò igórí ahón (ẹ̀yìn ahón) nígbà tí a ń pè é. Àfipè 'igórí ahón' ń ṣàpèjúwe ibi tí ahón ń lé séfín êyín ẹnu fún àsúnsí. 'Ètè òkè' ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa ète àgbé tó bá pípè ohùn bíi /p/ tàbí /b/ mu. 'Àjà enu' àti 'eka kòmóòkun' kì í ṣe àfipè ìbùdó àsúnsí.

Nínú kíkọ lẹ́tà, adírési (àdírẹ́ẹ̀sì) ni a kọ kí ó tó ohun kíkéde mìíràn — a máa ń fi sí ẹ̀gbẹ́ ọ̀tún lórí ìwé. Déèti máa ń tẹ̀lé adírési, lẹ́hìn náà ikíni, tí àkọlé ìdárò tàbí orí-òrò sì máa ń wà. Àwọn ọmọ akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ máa ń darú sí 'ikíni' fún ìgbésẹ̀ àkọ́kọ́ ṣùgbọ́n adírési ló ṣáájú gbogbo rẹ̀.

Àròko aláriyànjiyàn ló máa ń ní ihà méjì nítorí ó ń jiyàn koko kan tí a le gbà gba tàbí kọ̀. Ọ̀wọ̀ ojú-ẹnu méjì yìí — ìdálẹ́bi àti ìdálẹ́jọ — ni ó jẹ́ àdánidá fun irú àròko yìí. Asàpèjúwe máa ń ṣàpèjúwe kan ṣoṣo, asòtàn máa ń sọ ìtàn pẹ̀lú ọ̀nà kan, alálàyé sì máa ń ṣàlàyé ìmọ̀ kan laisi pípinnu alátakò.

Ohùn [w] jẹ́ kóńsónánti tó ń ṣe àmúlò ibùdó méjì pọ̀ — ète (fètèpè) àti ẹ̀yìn ahón tó lé séfín-ẹnu rọ̀ (àfàfà). Àfipè 'àfàfàséfètèpè' ṣopọ̀ àwọn ibùdó méjì wọ̀nyí papọ̀ fún [w]. Àfèji-ètèpè ń ṣàpèjúwe ohùn ète nìkan bíi /m/ tàbí /b/. Àfèrigipè ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa pípè eyin àti ète, bíi [f] tàbí [v].

Ìdàpọ̀ 'Ará oko' sí 'Aróoko' jẹ́ àpẹẹrẹ àrầnmó — èyíni ni dídàpọ̀ ọ̀rọ̀ méjì tàbí jù bẹ́ẹ̀ lọ papọ̀ láti ṣẹ̀dá ọ̀rọ̀ tuntun kan. Iyópo ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa bí ohùn kan ṣe máa ń yí ohùn tó sún mọ́ ọ, kò sì ṣẹlẹ̀ níbí. Isúnki ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa dídín ọ̀rọ̀ kúrú. Ìpajẹ ń sọ̀rọ̀ nípa pípa ohùn rẹyìn kúrò láìsí àrọ́pò.

Ọ̀rọ̀ 'ipèkun' ní sílébù mẹ́ta: i, pè, kun. Sílébù tó parí rẹ̀ ni 'ku' tí ó jẹ́ KF — kóńsónánti [k] àti fáwèlì [u] — ìní ìdánimọ̀ ìgbẹ̀yìn Yorùbá tó wọ́pọ̀. Àmúlò [n] tó kọjá lẹ́yìn jẹ́ ohùn imú onísílébù tí ó yàtọ̀ sí sílébù 'ku'. KFN yóò ti jẹ́ bí sílébù náà bá ní kóńsónánti, fáwèlì, àti ohùn imú papọ̀ láìsí ìwọ̀n.

In Yoruba morphology, the [o] in 'ogbon' is a bound morpheme that cannot stand alone — it must attach to a base to carry meaning, which is what àfarahe (C) describes. Àfibò (A) refers to a suffix, an affix added at the end of a word, but [o] appears at the beginning and functions differently. Ipilè (B) is the root or base morpheme, but [o] is not the core root of 'ogbon' — it is an attached element. Adádúró (D) means a free-standing or independent morpheme, which contradicts the fact that [o] here cannot function alone.

The vowel sound in Yoruba 'on' is an open-mid back rounded vowel, represented in phonetic transcription by the symbol [c] (equivalent to IPA [ɔ]), making A correct. This sound is produced with the mouth more open than when pronouncing a plain [o], giving it a distinct quality recognizable in many Yoruba words. [i] (B) is a front high vowel, completely different in place and manner of articulation from the vowel in 'on'. [u] (C) is a back high rounded vowel, also not matching the open quality of the 'on' vowel. [EE] (D) does not correspond to any standard phonetic symbol for this vowel in Yoruba phonology.

Modern Yoruba orthography demands precise tone marks on each syllable and correct vowel representation, and 'Wádií' (C) applies the correct high tones and vowel length that match the word's pronunciation. Option A (Wàdí) and B (Wàdi) both place a low tone on the first syllable 'wa', which does not reflect the actual pronunciation of this word. Option D (Wáidí) rearranges the vowels incorrectly, producing a different sequence of sounds that does not match the intended word. Correct tone marking is essential in Yoruba because changing a tone changes the meaning entirely.

In Yoruba noun phrase structure, oro-atókůn (determiners) are the word class that precede the head noun to specify or identify it, so A is correct. Orò-işe (B) refers to verbs, which do not occupy a position before nouns in a standard noun phrase. Oro-àpèjůwe (C) refers to adjectives, but unlike English, Yoruba adjectives typically follow the noun rather than precede it. Orò-åsopo (D) refers to conjunctions whose role is to link words or clauses, not to precede nouns in a phrase.

In Yoruba, 'Mo' means 'I', which is a first person singular pronoun — eni kínní (first person) eyo (singular) — making D the correct answer. Eni kínní òpo (A) is first person plural, which corresponds to 'Awa' meaning 'we', not 'Mo'. Eni keji eyo (C) is second person singular, referring to 'you' (one person), expressed in Yoruba as 'iwọ' or 'o'. Eni keji opo (B) is second person plural meaning 'you all', which in Yoruba is 'ẹ' or 'ẹyin', clearly different from 'Mo'.

In the sentence 'Olú n jeun pàlàpàlà', the word 'pàlàpàlà' describes the manner in which Olu is eating, functioning as an adverb (òrò-àpónlé), so A is correct. Adverbs in Yoruba modify verbs and appear after the verb phrase to tell us how an action is done. Òrò-àpėjúwe (B) refers to adjectives that modify nouns, but 'pàlàpàlà' is not describing any noun in this sentence. Orò-atókůn (C) refers to determiners that precede nouns, and orò-işe (D) refers to verbs — neither role applies to 'pàlàpàlà' here.

The best Yoruba equivalent of 'A word is enough for the wise' is 'Abò òrò là á so fómolúwàbi' (C), meaning half a word is sufficient for a person of good character — this captures the same wisdom using authentic Yoruba proverbial expression rather than a word-for-word translation. Options A and B attempt more literal renditions but do not reflect the natural proverbial form Yoruba speakers use. Option D is close to C in meaning but contains tonal inaccuracies in its phrasing. WAEC expects students to identify the culturally equivalent proverb, not just a grammatical translation.

The Yoruba aspect marker 'ti' indicates the perfective aspect (àşetán), showing that an action has been completed — in 'Ayo ti korin', Ayo has already finished singing, making A correct. Atererę (B) describes continuous or progressive aspect, typically marked in Yoruba by the particle 'ń', not 'ti'. Aişetán (C) refers to imperfective or incomplete aspect, which is the direct opposite of what 'ti' expresses. Bárakú (D) refers to habitual aspect, describing repeated or habitual actions, which is not what the use of 'ti' conveys.

Option D correctly translates 'He is trying to know the matter' because 'gbiyànjú' captures the effort of trying, and 'òkodoro orò' means the true reality or full substance of the matter. Options A and B use 'fé' which means 'want' or 'love', failing to convey the sense of active striving that 'trying' requires. Option C uses 'àtúnbotán' meaning the conclusion or end of a matter, which does not match 'the matter' in its full sense. Only D preserves both the effort ('gbiyànjú') and the depth of understanding ('òkodoro') that the original English sentence carries.

An àsipa òwe is a proverb with a paradoxical or ironic twist, and 'Ilé oba tó jó, ewà ló bù kun' (D) fits perfectly — the king's palace burning down yet being filled with beauty defies ordinary expectation, delivering deeper wisdom through surprise and contrast. Option A ('Ojú méwàá, kò jo ojú eni') expresses a general truth about self-interest but lacks the sharp ironic reversal that defines àsipa òwe. Option C ('Bá mi na omo mi, kò dénú olómo') makes a straightforward observation about parental feeling without the paradoxical structure required. The defining feature of D is how it turns an apparent disaster into something unexpected and meaningful.

Option C correctly translates 'I am delighted to hear from you' because 'Inú mi dùn' means 'I am delighted,' 'láti gbó' means 'to hear,' and 'orò tire' means 'your words/news specifically,' capturing the precise meaning of hearing from someone. Option A uses 'áti' instead of 'láti,' which is grammatically wrong in this context. Option B says 'orò re' instead of 'orò tire' — 'tire' is the emphatic possessive in Yoruba, making the meaning more exact and complete. Option D uses 'gbúró' which means to obey or listen, not the same as hearing from someone personally.

Agùntásoólò, meaning 'a sheep that walks alone,' is the correct answer because this proverb refers to a distinguished person who stands apart from the crowd and is therefore greeted with special honor. The phrase 'Eni gíga ni à ń kì ní' means 'it is a person of high standing that we greet,' and Agùntásoólò perfectly captures that idea of a unique, elevated individual. Atúnwonká refers to someone who recounts stories, Adúmáadán refers to a dark or mysterious person, and Afinjú refers to someone who is overly particular — none of these match the meaning of a highly respected person.

The expression 'Ó lówó lówó bí sèkèrè' is an àfiwé (simile) because it uses the Yoruba word 'bí' (meaning 'like' or 'as') to compare someone's wealth to a sekere, a beaded musical gourd. Simile always involves a direct comparison using a linking word, and 'bí' is the classic marker for simile in Yoruba. Àwítúnwí involves repetition for emphasis, which the doubling of 'lówó lówó' might suggest, but the overall structure with 'bí' confirms it is a comparison. Dídógba means equality or equivalence, which is too literal and does not capture the figurative nature of the expression.

Option A, 'Öpá tééré kanlè ó kànrun' (a thin stick falls on the ground and it bleeds), is an àló (riddle) because it presents a puzzling statement that requires the listener to think and provide an answer, such as a needle. Riddles in Yoruba are designed to challenge the mind with a mysterious description. Option B, 'Ojó re á dale,' is a warning or saying, not a riddle. Option C, 'Kì í burú títí kó má kenikan móni,' is an òwe (proverb) that offers wisdom rather than posing a puzzle.

Tortoise and Dog were friends because they belonged to the same egbé (club or association), which is the foundation of their relationship in this story. Membership in the same group creates bonds of loyalty and companionship in Yoruba culture. Their characters were not described as similar, which rules out Option B. Neither their physical strength nor their status as chiefs is presented as the reason for their friendship, so Options C and D are incorrect.

In the story 'Ijàpá àti Awon Eranko,' Ekùn (the Leopard) is the Baale (head chief) of the animals. In many Yoruba folktales, Ekùn holds authority among animals, unlike Western stories where the lion is always king. Kìnniún (Lion) is a common wrong guess because of its popular image as king in other traditions, but this specific Yoruba tale places Ekùn in authority. Erin (Elephant) and Efon (Buffalo) are powerful animals but do not hold the Baale title in this story.

Dog instructed Tortoise to bring enough yam to eat for one full month, making Option B correct. This detail is important because it shows the level of preparation and trust involved in their plan within the story. Option A says to bring only a small, carry-able amount, which contradicts the instruction. Option C simply says to bring many yams without the specific duration. Option D says not to bring more than one yam, which is the opposite of what Dog requested.

In Odù Ogúndá Méji from Abimbola's work, it is Ijòkùn who was prophesied to crack the kola nut. This prophecy is a specific detail within the Odu narrative and refers to a character central to that section of the poem. Orúnmilà is the deity of wisdom and divination who gives the prophecy, not the one who fulfills it. Ojolá is a python figure that appears elsewhere in the Odu. Kanranjágbón is connected to kola nut in a different context, making it a likely distractor.

Ifa instructed Òòyi òkókó to include òjolá (a python or boa constrictor) as one of the sacrifice items in Odù Ogúndá Méji. The prescription of specific animals and objects for sacrifice is a key element of Ifa poetry, and ojola features prominently in this Odu. Agbòn (wasp), adie (chicken), and obi (kola nut) are common sacrifice items in Ifa generally, but they are not what was specifically prescribed for Ooyi okoko in this particular verse of Ogunda Meji.

Ödàn (Odan, a type of fig tree) is one of the figures who cast divination for Erigi Àlo in Odù Ogúndá Méji. In Ifa literature, trees, animals, and natural elements are personified as diviners or characters who perform consultations. Igbó refers to the forest generally and is not identified as a diviner for Erigi Alo. Kanranjágbón and Ojolá appear elsewhere in the Odu but are not listed among those who divined for this particular character.

Dásofúnjó could not follow his friend on the journey because he had too many home responsibilities and obstacles weighing him down, which is what option D, 'idíwó ilé pò fún oun,' captures. His situation was not about his wife being ill (option A) or getting a new job at that time (option B), as neither of these was the reason given in the play. Option C suggesting he simply disliked travelling misrepresents his character, since his refusal was circumstantial, not a matter of personal preference. The play presents his home burdens as the genuine barrier, making D the only accurate answer.

In the play, Ojélàdé sent iyádùn-únní to bring a message or news for her, making option D the correct answer. Ańséétù (option A) and Ojékúnlé (option B) are characters in the drama but were not the ones sent on this errand. Dásofúnjó (option C) is a central character in the play but plays a different role in this scene. Understanding the relationships and roles of each character in Eégún Aláré is key to answering questions like this correctly.

Dúdúyemí is the main character, or olú èdá-itàn, of Eégún Aláré, making option B correct. Oje Láinnàká (option A) and Dásofúnjó (option C) are supporting characters who play important roles but are not the central figure around whom the story revolves. Ojélàdé (option D) is also a significant character but not the protagonist of the work. In Yoruba literary analysis, the olú èdá-itàn is the character whose journey and conflict drive the entire narrative forward.

Títí became pregnant for Jídé in the novel Olorunşogo, so option B is correct. Fémi (option A), Gbolá (option C), and Akin (option D) are all male characters in the story but are not the man responsible for Títí's pregnancy. The romantic and social entanglements in the novel are central to its plot, and confusing the characters is a common error students make. Knowing which character is linked to which event is essential for answering comprehension questions on this text.

Ogbéni Omódiyà was the lover of Lolá Ìbidùn in Olorunşogo, making option B the correct answer. Ogbéni Èsan (option A), Ogbéni Awé (option C), and Ogbéni Oláníyì (option D) are all characters who appear in the novel but none of them held this romantic role with Lolá Ìbidùn. The story explores relationships and their social consequences, so identifying the correct pairing of characters is important. Students who read the novel carefully would recognise Omódiyà as Lolá Ìbidùn's love interest.

Fúnké gave birth in the fifth week after her wedding, so the correct answer is option D, ösè karùn-ún. This detail is significant in the story because giving birth so soon after marriage raises questions about the circumstances of her pregnancy and creates social tension in the narrative. Options A through C, representing the second, third, and fourth weeks respectively, are all incorrect. The precise timing of this birth is a plot point that WAEC examiners frequently test to check how carefully students read the novel.

According to the poem, Aláàmù, the son of Şäiná, was told to first spend three years, méta, on the position or title, making option B correct. Two years (option A, méji) and four years (option C, mérin) are both wrong numbers that do not match the poem's content. Five years (option D, márùn-ún) is also incorrect. In the poem, this requirement of three years is a condition set before Aláàmù could fully enjoy or benefit from his position, and getting this number right shows a close reading of the ewì.

Aláàmù, son of Sàiná, was instructed to perform àsedànù, a sacrifice meant to avert misfortune or ward off evil consequences, making option C correct. Àseyorí (option A) refers to a sacrifice for success or achievement, which is the opposite of what was needed here. Option B, enu, does not fit this context as a type of sacrifice. Imowàáhù (option D) is also not the correct type of offering prescribed in this situation. Understanding the different types of sacrifices in Yoruba cultural and literary contexts helps students distinguish between these options.

In the poem Ori, the poet says that sugarcane, irèké, is the one that always gets into trouble with the farmer, olóko, making option C correct. This is a metaphorical statement about how something sweet or desirable often attracts problems from those who cultivate or control it. Atánràn (lightning, option A), agbálè (broom, option B), and abenilórí (headrest, option D) have no logical or poetic connection to sugarcane in this context. The image of the farmer having conflict with sugarcane reflects deeper themes in the poem about ori and personal destiny.

Ańwòó is the main character, or olú èdá-itàn, of Àpótí Alákàrà by Awé D., so option D is correct. Kàrímù (option A), Oyè (option B), and Abèó (option C) all appear in the drama but in supporting roles, not as the central figure. The title and plot of the play revolve around Ańwòó's story and experiences. Identifying the protagonist correctly requires familiarity with how the author has constructed the central conflict of the play around this character.

In the play Àpótí Alákàrà by D. Awé, Sààmú is one of the elderly members of Kàrímù's household and plays a significant role in the family setting. Àlàké, Adió, and Lálókun are other characters in the play but none of them holds the position of an elder in Kàrímù's home. Students must pay close attention to character roles when studying the prescribed drama text. Confusing supporting characters with household elders is a common mistake in this type of question.

Kàrímù chose owó sise, which means working for wages or engaging in paid labour, as his means of livelihood in the play. Farming (àgbè) and basket weaving (agbòn hihun) are occupations linked to other characters or to the general setting of the story. Teaching (olùkó) is also not the career path Kàrímù pursued according to the narrative. Understanding each character's occupation and motivation helps students answer drama-based questions accurately.

In Yoruba traditional culture, devotees of Oya (Olóya) are known to use edan, a sacred implement, during their religious activities and processions. Oníşàngó (Sango worshippers) are associated with the double-headed axe known as osé Sango, not edan. Babaláwo use divination tools such as the opele chain and ikin (palm nuts), while Eléégún refers to masquerade performers who belong to a different tradition entirely. Knowing which sacred objects belong to which deity or group is an important part of Yoruba cultural studies.

Sending ètù (a dark indigo-dyed cloth) as a coded message in Yoruba tradition signals that a secret has been uncovered or exposed (àşirí tú). This cloth carries symbolic meaning in traditional communication and is not used to announce the death of a king, the end of a fight, or an approaching war. Each of those events has its own distinct traditional symbol or announcement method. Students should study Yoruba cultural symbols carefully as they frequently appear in WAEC questions.

In Yoruba usage, orogún can be used to refer to a young woman who is a peer or rival in status, making it an appropriate substitute for omidan in certain contexts. Omoge is similar but more informal and colloquial, and while it resembles omidan in meaning, it is not considered the formal equivalent tested here. Ilémosú refers to a residential concept and has no connection to the meaning of omidan. İyáálé means the senior wife in a polygamous home, which is the opposite of an unmarried young woman.

Babátúndé is an àbikú name because it means father has returned, expressing the belief that a deceased father's spirit has been reborn in the newborn child. This name type belongs to a category called àbikú or àmútorunwá names, which reflect beliefs about the spirit world and reincarnation in Yoruba culture. Màlómo, Ekúndayò, and Ogínní are Yoruba names but they do not carry the specific àbikú identity. Recognising the meaning and category of traditional Yoruba names is a key skill for this exam.

In Yoruba tradition, the spirit or deity of the marketplace (òrisà ojà) is referred to as Egbon, meaning elder sibling, as a sign of respect and reverence for the protective force of the market. Bàbá (father), Ìyá (mother), and Ore (friend) are familiar terms of address but they are not the specific designation given to the market deity in Yoruba culture. This reflects how Yoruba people personify and assign familial roles to supernatural forces in their environment. Students must distinguish between general terms of address and specific traditional titles.

Within the Oro masquerade tradition of the Yoruba, the chief or head of the cult is given the title Erelú. Alápin-ín-ni, Ajànà, and Elegun are titles that belong to other Yoruba religious traditions and not to the Oro cult leadership. Elegun, for example, refers to a medium or vessel in Sango worship who becomes possessed by the deity. Students must match leadership titles to their correct cult or religious association to score well on Yoruba culture questions.

The passage states that Oyèjidé grows ewùrà and èsúrú, both of which are varieties of yam (isu), making option C the correct answer. The passage also explicitly says he does not grow kòkó or ògède, ruling out any confusion about his main crop. Agbàdo (maize) is the crop of his associate Àdisá, while gbágùúdá and ilá are the crops associated with Arèmú and Sùúrù. Reading comprehension questions require students to trace specific details to the correct character rather than applying general knowledge.

The passage focuses broadly on the farming community of Ibose, describing several farmers and their different crops alongside a theft incident, so Awọn àgbè Ibóse (Farmers of Ibose) is the title that captures the full scope of the passage. Oko (farm) is too vague and does not reflect the human dimension of the story. Ogbin àgbàdo is far too narrow since maize is only one of several crops mentioned and belongs to just one character. Awọn olè Ibóse is misleading because the thieves appear only as a subplot, not as the central subject of the passage.

Oru means nighttime, and the passage describes the thief working under cover of darkness — loading farm produce and attempting to flee before the farmers arrived and caught him. Thieves typically operate at night to avoid detection, and the dramatic scene of him being caught in the act fits oru perfectly. Àárò is morning, Iròlé is evening, and Ìdàjí refers to midday — none match the nighttime setting described in the passage.

The passage states 'Dérin a máa dáko rodo,' meaning Dérin farms near the riverside or stream. In Yoruba agricultural practice, riverside farming is closely associated with growing pepper (ata) because the crop thrives in moist, well-watered soil. Àdisá is clearly linked to àgbàdo (maize), Arèmú and Sùúrù enjoy gbágùúdá and ilá, and Oyèjídé cultivates yam — so Dérin is the only one whose farming activity points to pepper.

Asàpèjúwe means a descriptive essay, and 'Ìyá' (Mother) is a title that calls for describing the qualities, character, and role of a mother in detail. Oníròyin is a reportorial or journalistic essay, asotàn is a narrative story, and ajemó-isipayá is expository writing — none of these fit a title like 'Ìyá' which naturally invites description and characterisation.

In the passage, 'dode' means to run away from or escape — 'Púpò nínú àwon àgbè ibóse ti dode àwon olè náà' means many farmers had fled or escaped the thieves. 'Só' is the correct Yoruba word meaning to run or flee, making it the best synonym. 'Pa' means to kill, 'yo' means to come out or emerge in a different sense, and 'nà' means to flog or stretch — none carry the meaning of escaping from danger.

A létà gbèfe is an informal letter, and a letter to a friend (létà sí òré) is the classic example of informal writing because it uses casual, personal language without official structure. Letters to the police station, the Governor, and job application letters are all formal because they address institutions or authority figures and follow strict format and language conventions.

The phrase 'Bá mi kí gbogbo ilé' (Give my greetings to everyone at home) is a typical closing remark found in personal letters, making it belong to onílétà, which is letter-writing composition. Asàríyànjiyàn is argumentative, asàpèjúwe is descriptive, and oníròyìn is reportorial — none of them would naturally contain such a personal greeting that signals the end of a letter to someone known to the writer.

Asotàn is a narrative essay that tells a personal story or recounts an event, and 'Ìdíjé bóolù kan tí mo wò' (A football match I watched) is a first-person account of an experience — the hallmark of narrative writing. 'Jà ilú mi' and 'Owó ju omo lo' are argumentative or debate topics, while 'Igi òpę' (the palm tree) is a descriptive title — none of these invite personal storytelling the way a witnessed event does.

Afipè àsúnsí refers to labio-dental sounds, which are produced when the lower lip (ètè isàlè) makes contact with the upper teeth. The lower lip is the active articulator that moves to create these sounds, as seen with consonants like /f/. Ètè òkè (upper lip) is passive, àjà enu is the palate inside the mouth, and ògiri ofun is the back wall of the throat — none of these are involved in labio-dental articulation.

Kóńsónànti akùnyùn means voiced consonants — sounds produced with the vocal cords vibrating. Among the options, [g] is a voiced velar stop where the voice box is active during production. [h] is voiceless (no vocal cord vibration), [t] is a voiceless alveolar stop, and [kl] involves voiceless sounds — only [g] has the voicing quality that defines akùnyùn consonants.

In Yoruba, syllables typically follow a consonant-vowel (CV) or vowel-only (V) pattern, so 'agánnigàn' breaks down as a-gán-ni-gàn giving four syllables. Each vowel forms the nucleus of its own syllable, and consonants attach to the vowel that follows them. Option A (agán-nigàn) groups too many sounds together, option B (agán-ni-gàn) misplaces the first syllable boundary, and option D (a-gánni-gàn) incorrectly joins two separate syllables — only C respects Yoruba syllable structure.

Counting syllables in Yoruba requires identifying every vowel and every syllabic nasal (n/m that forms its own syllable). Breaking down 'Bèlèntàsé': Bè (1) - lè (2) - n (3, the nasal 'n' is a full syllable in Yoruba) - tà (4) - sé (5). That gives exactly five syllables, making Márùn-ún correct. Méfà (six) and above are wrong because students often miss that the standalone nasal 'n' counts as its own syllable.

When 'Rán aşo' contracts to 'ránso', the initial vowel 'a' of 'aşo' is completely dropped, not changed or fused. This process of deleting a vowel is called ipaje fáwéli (vowel deletion/elision). Iyópò fáwéli is wrong because that involves vowel harmony or substitution, not loss. Ijeyopò fáwéli refers to coalescence where two vowels merge into one, which did not happen here.

Àpètúnpè elébe means partial or light-syllable reduplication, where only the initial CV unit of a root is repeated to form a new word.
